visuals.heading: Three Things Make a Static Company List

items.text: The answer tells you how much support actually exists under the training-program language.
Instead of memorising a list of names, apply the same four checks to any company you are considering.
A genuinely fresher-friendly employer treats your first weeks or months as a real training period, not a formality before you get thrown at production work.
If nobody in the interview can describe what week one actually looks like, that is itself an answer.

blocks.heading: It Helps to Think in Categories

items.text: Large IT services firms typically run large-batch training programs with a fixed curriculum, assigned mentors, and a defined bench-to-billable pipeline.
Well-funded, professionally run startups often bring in one or two freshers per team rather than large batches, which can mean closer day-to-day mentorship and faster exposure to real decisions.
Most "best companies" content only talks about private-sector IT and startups.
Public sector undertakings (PSUs) hire freshers mainly through GATE scores, and government departments hire through exams like SSC CGL, IBPS (banking), or state-level recruitment boards.

Global Capability Centres (GCCs), the India-based teams that multinational companies run for their own product, engineering, or analytics work, have expanded sharply and often invest heavily in structured fresher training, since they are building long-term local capability, not just cheap headcount.

blocks.heading: Research a Company Before You Accept

items.text: This is the part most freshers skip because the offer letter feels final and the clock feels urgent.
A handful of five-star reviews posted in the same week often means an internal review drive, not organic sentiment.
"How is the culture?" invites a generic answer.

blocks.heading: Skill Portfolio, and Your Future Income

items.text: Here is the part a brand-name-driven list never tells you: the biggest return from your first job is not the starting salary.
A genuinely good employer for a fresher builds more than a technical skill list.
Not just the tools listed in the job description, the specific technical and role skills that combination of employer and team will actually let you practice in year one.

blocks.heading: Freshers Make When Picking a First Employer

items.text: Two people joining the same company in different teams can have completely different first-year experiences.

A slightly higher starting salary at a company with no structured training and high early attrition can cost you more over two or three years than a lower starting offer with a genuine mentor-pairing program that accelerates your skill and your next negotiation.
Any individual data point can be an outlier in either direction.

visuals.heading: Questions Before Choosing

blocks.heading: Did Interviewers Show Up on Time

items.text: Could the person hiring you clearly describe what your first project or first few weeks would look like, without vague deflection.
Did anyone mention who your day-to-day point of contact would be if you got stuck, or was support left.
Were expectations around hours, deadlines, and review cycles stated plainly, or only hinted at through phrases like "fast-paced" without specifics.
